source.title: Breaking the Block: Preserving Data Continuity to Train Superior SAEs for Instruct Models
source.authors: Jia-Ming Li; Hao-Ran Ye; Yu-Kun Chen; Xin-Yu Li; Lei Zhang; H. Alinejad-Rokny; Jimmy Chih-Hsien Peng; Min Yang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation affecting the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies SAE training data and sequence-boundary handling, and measures reconstruction, model-loss preservation, and gradient noise. These results bear on whether SAE reconstruction errors depend on training choices, but do not analyze dark-matter error structure directly.
record.gate_note: The study does not test whether SAE errors are linearly predictable, compare errors token-by-token across SAE sizes, or test reconstruction against equal-sized random errors. Its feature-steering examples do not measure the contribution of the omitted SAE error. Rows below capture relevant training-method, reconstruction, preservation, and controlled-prefix results; cited results are excluded.
record.test_reason: This is an SAE training-method paper. It compares its own method, FAST, which trains on independent chat instances, with block-training baselines on MSE, Delta Loss, KL and GSNR. It never analyses the structure of the SAE error: no linear prediction of the error, no per-token comparison across sizes, no random-error control, and no linear/nonlinear split. It also never cites or tests the dark-matter claim. Lower MSE from training-data choices is not evidence about V6, because no part of the error is identified as dark matter versus learnable features. The gain is also confounded by matching the training data to the evaluation data: evaluation uses chat dialogues, while BT(P) trains on the Pile. The rows are the study's own method against baselines, and GSNR is a gradient-noise diagnostic, not an error measure.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that block training introduces attention-contamination gradient noise for instruct-model SAEs. They report that FAST raises GSNR, reconstruction fidelity (MSE, Delta Loss, KL) and feature interpretability. The steering claim is stronger than 'can affect': they say steering special-token features at moderate coefficients improves generation quality, with an inverted-U relationship.
record.recipe_differences: This paper studies FAST versus block-training paradigms for training SAEs on instruct-model data; it does not reproduce the original dark-matter error analysis or its linear-predictability and scaling measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The training data/sequence-boundary method changes outcomes; the paper also reports different effects across model, layer, SAE architecture, expansion factor, context length, and training step. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, FAST has worse KL divergence at the reported layer/configuration despite better special-token MSE and near-zero Delta Loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Training SAEs on independent, chat-formatted instances (FAST) cuts reconstruction MSE and Delta Loss on instruct models sharply, compared with block training on the Pile or on concatenated chat data. Example: Qwen2.5-3B-it Delta Loss falls from +51.43% to -0.04%. There is one KL exception (Qwen2.5-7B-it, layer 20).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The size of SAE reconstruction error on instruct models depends strongly on whether the training data's format and instance boundaries match the evaluation distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Prepending an unrelated 512-token prefix lowers the GSNR of SAE training gradients compared with clean FAST training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-instance attention contamination adds gradient noise to SAE training on instruct models.

record.problems: The paper does not directly measure dark-matter residual structure. Delta Loss and KL divergence are reported for selected configurations; no uncertainty estimates are provided. The controlled-prefix experiment measures GSNR, not whether the resulting SAE error is linearly predictable or how its token-level distribution changes.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed SAE MSE results across other model/layer/expansion combinations in Tables 6–13 and figures 5 and 7, and the early-step GSNR comparison in Table 1, were not individually extracted; representative reconstruction results and the controlled-prefix GSNR sweep are retained. Feature-interpretability scoring and steering results do not measure the claim versions’ named error properties.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of the SAE error from input activations is not examined.
No per-token error-norm prediction across SAE sizes and no same-context failure analysis. Expansion factors 8X and 16X are compared only on aggregate MSE.
No comparison of reconstruction loss against equal-norm random errors.
No split of the error into linear and nonlinear components.
Steering experiments do not measure what is lost when the error term is dropped.

Shows that aggregate MSE and Delta Loss depend on training-data handling. It does not test whether the residual error that remains is a training artifact or structure in the model's representation. Sparsity penalty, shrinkage, dead latents and end-to-end training are not isolated.

record.verdict_notes: The paper never mentions SAE dark matter or the original source. The reader's 'tests/T5' with V6 supports is not justified: lower aggregate MSE from better-matched training data does not show the residual error is an artifact rather than model structure. All rows are own-method versus baseline comparisons or gradient diagnostics. The baselines' disadvantage is partly a train/eval distribution mismatch, since evaluation uses 5,000 held-out dialogues from the FAST data.

versions.untested_parts: Linear predictability of the SAE error vector from input activations.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, same-context failures, and whether error norms persist with scale.
No comparison of model-loss harm from SAE reconstruction against random errors of the same size.
No separation of linear and nonlinear dark-matter components, or test of their learning behavior.
No measurement of behavior lost by omitting the SAE error term from feature-based analyses.

The study varies data continuity and SAE training method, and compares SAE architectures, but does not isolate sparsity penalty, shrinkage, dead latents, or end-to-end training as causes of dark matter; nor does it directly measure dark-matter structure.

reader_labels.condition: FAST versus block-training results in the Table 14 Delta Loss configurations, the Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct context-length ablation, special-token MSE on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and controlled-prefix GSNR comparisons
reader_labels.reason: Changing SAE training/data continuity is associated with substantially improved reconstruction or preservation metrics, and adding unrelated prefixes lowers GSNR; see r1–r22 and r25–r46.
